1:
Whose psalm this is divides them further than anything in it. Clarke canvasses the occasions and prefers David's Ammonite victory, with the crown of Rabbah on his own head, to the guesses of Sennacherib's defeat or Hezekiah's added fifteen years. Delitzsch reports that the Targum and Talmud read it of the king Messiah, and that Rashi thought the Messianic reading ought rather to be given up for the Christians' sake; he settles for David, whose cause, moving through suffering to triumph, is figuratively that of Christ. Calvin keeps the thanksgiving David's while holding the Spirit's design was above all to direct the faithful to Christ, the end and perfection of this kingdom. Spurgeon simply begins there: Jesus is a royal personage, King over minds and hearts, proclaimed so even on the cross. Gill reads every clause of the King Messiah. Ellicott refuses the move, insisting an allusion to the eternal kingdom is not to be forced on the passage.

What was asked and granted comes next. Ellicott renders the opening as a present, the king is exulting in thy might, and notices that the word for request occurs nowhere else, being connected with a root meaning to be poor and so in want, with an emphatic negative: the request of his lips thou hast by no means withheld. He finds the evidence pulling two ways, a prayer for length of life suggesting sickness while the psalm's tone suggests victory. Delitzsch pairs it with the psalm before, where the people brought wishes and prayers for their king and here bring thanksgiving and hope. Henry observes that no prayer is accepted but what is the heart's desire, and that returns of prayer call for returns of praise. Calvin adds that David could have thanked God privately but meant to testify that his blessings redounded to the public good.

The preventing and the crown occupy the third verse. Clarke takes the verb back to its Latin, to go before, as in the collect asking God to prevent us in all our doings, and as older English used God before, which he illustrates from a royal speech before Agincourt; Ellicott reaches for the same collect. Wesley has the king crowned with more blessings and sooner than he expected. Gill turns the earliness into doctrine, the blessings put into Christ's hands before he was manifest in the flesh. On the crown Clarke and Delitzsch agree on the Ammonite diadem of Rabbah, renowned for its weight of gold, Delitzsch adding that the verse cannot mean a first coronation but the increase of a kingship's honour. Ellicott lists the candidates, Rabbah, a coronation, Ewald's birthday, and settles for a symbol of victory, maidens being accustomed to meet a monarch returning in triumph with a garland.

Life, glory and blessing close the half. Clarke grants that the fourth verse has made some read the psalm of Hezekiah's recovery, but prefers the Messiah, of whom David was the type and in several respects the representative; Ellicott answers that for ever and ever is merely a term for indefinite length, like the common salutation of a king. Wesley takes it both ways, a long reign here and a translation afterwards, fulfilled more eminently in one who asked to be saved from death and was given a nobler life. On the glory Clarke says that great as it was its greatness came from God's salvation, there being no true nobility but of the soul; Delitzsch has that help itself pave the way to honour. The sixth verse both Clarke and Gill render literally, thou hast set him for blessings, Clarke making him the source whence all are drawn and Gill naming redemption, righteousness and sanctification; Delitzsch calls it a stronger form of the word to Abram, a blessing both possessed and passed on. Ellicott prefers in thy presence to with thy countenance, which Wesley makes a smile of grace and favour.
7:
The seventh verse is the hinge. Ellicott notes that the psalm has until now addressed Jehovah and here turns in prophetic strain to the king; Delitzsch marks the same place as the opening of the second half, and insists the change carries confident expectation rather than wish. Spurgeon takes the trusting king for a master in the use of the weapons, handling well the shield of faith, safe in his Father's care until his hour came, committing his cause to him that judgeth right and at the last his spirit into the same hands. A holy confidence in Jehovah, he says, is the true mother of victories, and though the psalm was composed long before the conflict, faith overleaps time and chants her triumph while still singing her battle song. Henry makes the verse the ground of the people's courage, as the first verse was the ground of their thanks. Gill cites the Targum for the King Messiah, and Clarke disclaims skill and valour for faith in a conquering arm, and reads the immovability of David's prototype, whose throne remains for ever.

The enemies are then found out, by an uncontrollable power, Clarke says, that reaches them wherever hidden, since God knows the secret sinner. Gill unrolls who they are, from the Jews who would not have him reign and the Gentiles concerned in his death, through the Roman emperors and the followers of the man of sin, to professors who oppose him in practice, and the devil with his angels; the finding rests on omniscience, he says, and the holding on omnipotence. Henry defines them as those who hate him, hated because God had set him apart and hated again because they hated the light, in both cases without just cause and God hated through them.

The oven divides them. Ellicott calls the figure most obscure as it stands, gets the sense by a very slight change to thou shalt put them into a fiery oven, and takes the image not from Sodom but, since the Philistines treated enemies so, from a smelter's furnace. The time of thine anger is literally of thy face, and he observes that a power of withering the wicked with a glance, usually ascribed to the face of God, is here given to his representative, until the poet, startled by his own boldness, refers it back to Jehovah, whose wrath is literally his nostril. Delitzsch reads the face the same way, as the personal appearing of the king, and grounds the verse in history: the arrival of David decided the fall of Rabbath Ammon, whose people were put under instruments of torture and cast into brick-kilns, and the prospect here is moulded on that fate. Gill reports the brick-kiln and Sodom guesses, prefers put them into, and finds fulfilment at the fall of Jerusalem and in a later burning of Babylon. Clarke makes one class of sinners the means of consuming another before perishing itself; Wesley says only that they go like wood cast in.

The tenth and eleventh verses turn on grammar. Ellicott gives their fruit more fully as fruit of the womb, reads the eleventh verse as a concession rather than a reason, though they have intended evil they have no power at all. Delitzsch glosses the inclining of evil as putting it over a man so that it may fall in upon him. Wesley and Clarke both take the fruit for children and posterity, so that the memorial perishes with root and branch. Gill holds that the intention of evil is itself evil and punishable. Henry hears the designs aimed higher than the throne: those who aimed to unking David aimed in effect to un-God Jehovah.
12:
The turned back is read four ways. Ellicott gives the Hebrew literally as thou shalt put them shoulder, quoting the Vulgate for it, and continues upon thy strings thou shalt aim against the face of them; he records a rendering shalt strike them back but thinks the English version explains rightly, comparing the older phrase about giving an enemy the neck. Delitzsch calls making them into a back, that is, into such as turn the back to you, a more choice expression than the usual idiom, and glosses the evil of the verse before as inclined down over a man so that it may fall in upon him. Gill offers three senses: they flee to hiding places from the wrath of God and of the Lamb, to no purpose; or God turns his own back, disregarding them when they cry in their destruction; or, as the Targum inclines, they are set together on one side and separated from the people of God, as the Christians were brought out of Jerusalem before its fall. Clarke reads panic instead, since God can strike the most numerous army even in its moment of victory, so that the lame take the prey and the enemy turns as though a volley of arrows had been discharged in its face.

The last verse turns back to God, as Ellicott notes, and he would render its close we will both with song and lyre celebrate thy power. Delitzsch hears the shape of the whole psalm in it: having spread its wings in twice three tetrastichs the song closes by soaring aloft and losing itself in a distich, and what it asks is victory in battle for the king, be thou exalted meaning manifest thyself in thy supernal and judicial sovereignty, the might longed for being one before which everything opposing must yield, and for which a joyous gratitude is promised in advance. Clarke turns the imperative round: exalt thyself, for thy creatures cannot exalt thee, and God can give victory over the most formidable enemies though his people strike not one blow in their own defence but stand still to see his salvation. Gill finds the exertion fulfilled three times over, at the destruction of Jerusalem when the kingdom of God came with power, again when Babylon falls because strong is the Lord who judges her, and finally at the day of judgment. Wesley says only that it is by his own power, or the manifestation of it.

Clarke alone asks which power is to be praised, and answers that God is praised in reference to whatever attribute he has shown most in defending his followers. One man wants teaching, prays for it, is deeply instructed, and will naturally celebrate wisdom. Another finds himself beset by adversaries he cannot cope with, cries to the Almighty for strength, is heard and strengthened in his soul, and so magnifies all-conquering power. A third feels himself lost and on the brink, calls for mercy, is heard and saved, and makes mercy the burden of his song. He ends with the old Anglo-Scottish Psalter, which has it that we shall make known his words in good will and good work, for he sings well that works well, and that the doubled promise to sing stands once for the love of the heart and once for the showing of righteousness as an example.
